title: Evaluate Agent Behavior with Evidence
audience: Practitioners deciding whether an agent change is safe and useful enough to release using repeatable, evidence-backed comparisons.
learningObjectives: Turn product requirements and failure history into versioned evaluation cases.
Score final outcomes, tool trajectories, policy compliance, cost, and latency with explicit rubrics.
Combine deterministic checks, human review, and model graders without treating any grader as ground truth.
Compare a candidate with a baseline and make a documented release decision.

segments.spokenText: Welcome. This class replaces impressive agent demos with repeatable release evidence. You will define testable behavior claims, build representative and adversarial cases, score outcomes and trajectories, compare a candidate with a baseline, and turn production failures into governed regression tests.
segments.stageDirection: Display the evaluation lifecycle from claim through release decision and regression intake.

segments.spokenText: An evaluation is a repeatable experiment, not a guided demonstration. Start with a claim that evidence can confirm or reject. Identify the workflow and configuration version, target population, expected outcome, unacceptable behavior, scoring rules, sample, environment, budgets, and release threshold before running the candidate. Separate task success from style, safety, policy compliance, efficiency, and user experience. A pleasant answer may violate authority. A safe trajectory may still produce an unusable result. One average cannot express both. Give every case a stable identifier, slice, versioned input fixture, observable expected outcome, allowed tool trajectory, forbidden behavior, rubric, and latency, cost, turn, or retry budget. Predeclared claims and thresholds reduce the temptation to redefine success after seeing results.
segments.stageDirection: Build a versioned evaluation-case contract and separate six scoring dimensions.

visual.description: A case contract binds workflow version, fixture, expected outcome, allowed trajectory, forbidden behavior, rubric, and budgets.
visual.altText: Each case has a stable ID and slice plus versioned inputs, observable outcomes, permitted tools, prohibited behavior, scoring criteria, and resource limits.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Present the complete contract as one static form.

segments.spokenText: Build a set that reflects the product, not merely what is easy to pass. Include common tasks, important user journeys, supported languages and modalities, high-impact groups, difficult long-tail cases, and actual data distributions. Preserve a holdout set so repeated tuning does not overfit every known example. Add boundaries and adversarial conditions: ambiguous intent, prompt injection, missing permission, stale or conflicting evidence, malformed tool output, timeouts, unsafe requests, and policy conflicts. Every confirmed production incident should yield the smallest reproducing case after privacy review. Synthetic generation can broaden coverage, but a human must decide whether each synthetic case represents a real product behavior or risk. Track source, consent, transformation, retention, and slice membership so a case remains governed and interpretable.
segments.stageDirection: Fill a ten-case matrix with representative, boundary, adversarial, and prior-failure slices.

visual.description: A coverage matrix balances common, boundary, adversarial, and incident-derived cases.
visual.altText: Four representative, two boundary, two adversarial, and two prior-failure cases cover important journeys and critical risks.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show all case slices and coverage labels in a static matrix.

segments.spokenText: Score both what happened and how it happened. Deterministic graders fit schemas, exact constraints, calculations, permission decisions, tool arguments, postconditions, terminal states, and latency or cost budgets. Human reviewers fit nuanced usefulness, clarity, and context-dependent judgment when guided by an explicit rubric and blinded to candidate identity. Model graders can add scalable signals, but they are not ground truth. Calibrate them against human-labeled examples, version their prompts and models, measure agreement by slice, and route material disagreement for review. For agent runs, inspect tool choice, input validation, approvals, authority, retry count, evidence preservation, handoffs, verification, and final state. A correct final sentence can hide a forbidden tool call or duplicate write. An imperfect but safely contained run may reveal a recoverable product defect instead of a safety failure.
segments.stageDirection: Score one run across outcome, trajectory, policy, safety, latency, cost, and grader evidence.

visual.description: A multi-lane rubric separates final outcome from trajectory, policy, safety, latency, cost, and grader confidence.
visual.altText: Deterministic checks, blinded human review, and calibrated model signals contribute separate evidence to a scored run.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Display all rubric lanes and evidence sources simultaneously.

segments.spokenText: Consider an agent that creates a correct support summary. The final-answer grader awards full points. The trajectory check finds that the agent queried an unrelated customer record, skipped approval, and retried a write after an unknown timeout. Permission and postcondition checks fail, so the case is a critical failure despite the polished summary. A second run asks for clarification, stays within one account, records approval, and stops after a provider error. It earns fewer usefulness points but passes safety and recovery criteria. This comparison shows why one overall impression is not a release gate.
segments.stageDirection: Compare a polished unsafe trajectory with a less polished but bounded and recoverable trajectory.

visual.description: Two runs with similar outputs receive different release outcomes because their trajectories differ.
visual.altText: The polished run fails permission, approval, and retry checks. The bounded run requests clarification, preserves authority, and stops safely.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show both scored run records side by side.

segments.spokenText: Compare baseline and candidate on identical case versions, fixtures, environment, budgets, grader definitions, and sampling rules. Report pass rate and score distribution by slice, not only a global mean. Include critical failures, grader disagreement, latency percentiles, cost per successful task, retries, and uncertainty. Before the run, declare must-not-regress slices and the minimum practical improvement that justifies change. A higher average cannot excuse a new permission bypass, cross-tenant disclosure, uncontrolled purchase, or unreconciled write. Investigate changed cases individually and record whether the difference comes from model behavior, prompt, tool, retrieval, policy, orchestration, or infrastructure. The release decision is ship, hold, or rollback with named evidence, reviewer, residual risk, and follow-up work. Safety, authority, and high-impact behavior require accountable human sign-off.
segments.stageDirection: Compare candidate and baseline by slice with hard critical gates and a signed disposition.

visual.description: A release table combines slice metrics, critical gates, uncertainty, cost, latency, and human disposition.
visual.altText: Candidate improvements are accepted only when must-not-regress safety and permission slices pass and practical improvement exceeds the declared threshold.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Present the complete baseline-candidate table and gate results statically.

segments.spokenText: Make evaluation a controlled learning loop. Privacy-reviewed production traces, explicit feedback, escalations, and incidents can reveal cases the offline set missed. Remove or transform sensitive content while preserving the behavior that caused failure. Apply consent, access, retention, deletion, and provenance requirements before adding anything to the corpus. Version the case, fixture, expected behavior, rubric, deterministic checks, model-grader configuration, workflow, tools, policies, environment, and results. Keep prior versions so release and rollback decisions remain reproducible. Monitor case duplication, slice balance, label quality, grader drift, and holdout contamination. A dashboard score without the inputs and decision rules that produced it is an observation, not durable release evidence.
segments.stageDirection: Move a privacy-reviewed incident through minimization, case review, regression intake, versioning, and future release use.

visual.description: Production evidence becomes a governed regression case without retaining unnecessary sensitive content.
visual.altText: Incident evidence is minimized, reviewed, versioned, added to the proper slice, and protected from holdout contamination.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the entire governed intake sequence as a static flow.

segments.spokenText: Choose one agent workflow. Write the release claim, one must-not-regress slice, its observable threshold, and one trajectory failure that a final-answer score would miss.
segments.stageDirection: Display four fields for claim, critical slice, threshold, and hidden trajectory failure.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Create a predeclared evaluation claim and critical trajectory gate.

segments.stageDirection: Hold the evaluation worksheet for up to ninety seconds with pause, extend, transcript, and continue controls.

segments.spokenText: Checkpoint. The candidate improves the average score but fails one critical permission case. May the team ship because the aggregate improved?
segments.stageDirection: Show the improved mean beside the failed must-not-regress permission slice.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Hold or fix the release because a predeclared critical gate failed.

segments.stageDirection: Hold the checkpoint for up to sixty seconds with accessible response and extend controls.

segments.spokenText: Do not ship on the average. Honor the must-not-regress permission gate, inspect the failed case, and record a hold or rollback until the violation is corrected and retested. If you chose to adjust the case weight after the result, return to the predeclared threshold; post-hoc weighting makes the decision untrustworthy. If you rejected every candidate regression, refine the rule: noncritical tradeoffs may be accepted when thresholds, uncertainty, reviewer approval, and residual risk are explicit.
segments.stageDirection: Reveal Critical gate overrides mean, Investigate, and Retest before disposition.

feedback.correct: You preserved the predeclared critical-slice gate instead of rationalizing an unsafe average.
feedback.retry: Check whether any must-not-regress behavior failed before considering aggregate improvement.

segments.spokenText: Open the agent evaluation activity. Build ten versioned cases, a 100-point rubric, and deterministic checks for schema, permissions, postconditions, turns, latency, and cost. Blind-score baseline and candidate, review disagreement by slice, choose ship, hold, or rollback using predeclared thresholds, and add one failure to the regression set.
segments.stageDirection: Display the case set, rubric, grader definitions, comparison report, and signed release decision.
Provide one hundred eighty seconds of optional work time with pause, extend, save, transcript, and continue controls.

segments.spokenText: When ready, begin the knowledge check. You will place thresholds before results, score agent trajectories, calibrate model graders, enforce critical slices, and identify the versions required for reproducibility.
segments.stageDirection: Show Review class, Return to activity, and Begin knowledge check.

segments.spokenText: Predeclare the claim, cover reality and failure, score outcome and trajectory, compare identical cases, honor critical gates, and preserve every version needed to reproduce the decision.
segments.stageDirection: Display the six evaluation rules beside the signed release decision.
